newsitem.title: UK: "Tidal flow" of copper seen between LME and China.
newsitem.headline: "Tidal flow" of copper seen between LME and China.

text.p: A "tidal flow" of 200,000 tonnes of copper goes backwards and forwards between the London Metal Exchange (LME) and Chinese bonded warehouses, industry specialists Bloomsbury Minerals Economics (BME) said.
In its latest monthly report, BME analyst Peter Hollands looked at various episodes of unexpected large swings of some 200,000 tonnes in LME warehouse stocks.
The most recent is occuring now, with inventories having fallen from end-August 1996 levels of 275,000 tonnes to just over 90,000 tonnes.
But between end-January and end-July 1994, there was also a 260,000-tonne decrease, while from end-July 1995 to end-January 1996 inventories increased 200,000 tonnes, BME said.
At the times these movements were thought to represent fundamental shifts between surplus and deficit.
But BME said that what could be happening is that various Chinese agencies acquired a stockpile of 200,000 tonnes of refined copper in early 1994.
Some of this has been sold off in tranches of around 85,000 tonnes and subsequently re-acquired, alongside various similar operations with scrap.
However, not all the drawdowns now taking place represent stockpile operations, BME said.
"We have clearly been under-estimating long-term consumption growth," it said.
Cathode and scrap stocks in China and south-east Asia have been depleted, while short-term consumption was also under-estimated.
"But at least half and possibly over three-quarters of the LME stock drawdown represents re-location to the Chinese Reserve, we believe," BME said.
The overall market balance is now switching to a small surplus, and if surplus stocks build up on the LME prices will gradually trend lower.
However, if the Chinese Reserve absorbs the surplus, and if consumption growth is under-estimated there may be a tiny deficit in 1997 and higher prices, it added.
